articles.title: Argentina's Milei threatens UK with international legal action over Falkland Islands oil project
articles.summary: A major offshore oil project is opening a new front in the Falklands sovereignty dispute, with Buenos Aires threatening legal action and sanctions against companies involved.

image.caption: Milei spoke at the UN General Assembly in New York days before threatening international legal action against the UK (FILE: 23/09/2026)Image: CNP/AdMedia/picture alliance

blocks.text: Argentine President Javier Milei on Monday gave the United Kingdom two weeks to halt an oil project near the Falkland Islands or face international legal action.
The potentially lucrative project has intensified the long-running sovereignty dispute as the islands prepare for oil production that could transform their small economy.
What has Argentina threatened to do?
Milei said Argentina would take the dispute to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg if the UK did not halt the Sea Lion project within two weeks.

"I instructed the Foreign Ministry and our legal teams to initiate arbitration proceedings against the United Kingdom for the illegal sacking of our resources through the Sea Lion Project in the North Falklands Basin," Milei wrote on X.
"If within two weeks the United Kingdom does not stop the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea," he added.
Argentina argues that Britain's authorization of oil exploration violates a UN resolution calling on both sides to refrain from unilateral actions while their sovereignty dispute remains unresolved.

blocks.caption: Port Stanley is the capital of the British-controlled Falkland Islands, which Argentina claims as the Malvinas (FILE: 07/10/2019)Image: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

blocks.text: Milei has also threatened to bar companies involved in unauthorized oil exploration around the Falklands from operating in Argentina's oil and mining sectors.
His government has sent Argentina's Congress a bill proposing prison terms of up to 20 years for extracting resources around the islands without Argentine authorization.
Argentine authorities say they are investigating at least 60 companies and executives for possible violations.
What is the Sea Lion oil project?
Sea Lion is a major offshore oil field around 220 kilometers (137 miles) north of the Falkland Islands.
The project is being developed by Israel's Navitas Petroleum and Britain's Rockhopper Exploration under licenses issued by the Falkland Islands authorities.
Oil production is expected to begin in 2028.
The companies have rejected Argentina's objections, saying they hold valid licenses for the project.

blocks.caption: Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war over the Falkland Islands in 1982 after Argentine forces invaded the British-controlled territory [FILE: 1982]Image: PA/empics/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The UK has also defended the right of the Falkland Islanders to develop their natural resources.
Why are the Falkland Islands disputed?
The Falkland Islands have been under British control since 1833, but Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago, which it calls the Malvinas.
Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, triggering a 10-week war with the UK.
The conflict killed 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British service members and three islanders before British forces retook the territory.
The UK says the islanders have the right to determine their own future.
In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters backed remaining a British Overseas Territory, with turnout of about 92%.
Argentina rejects the referendum and maintains its sovereignty claim.

articles.title: UK: US government questions bail for Fairford base suspects
articles.summary: The US government sees "the hand of a foreign actor" in the security scare at RAF Fairford, a hub for US heavy bombers in Europe. Donald Trump criticized the suspects being released on bail amid…

image.caption: Police sealed off the area near the air base amid Sunday's operation Image: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The US government has described the security alert over the weekend at the RAF Fairford base in southern England as a "very serious situation," thanking UK authorities for their cooperation.
But President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio also both questioned the move to grant the five suspects bail under strict conditions as investigations against them continue.

RAF Fairford is a major military air field fairly close to the south coast of England. It's a rare European base from which the US operates heavy bombers, with the range to reach Iran amid the current conflict in the Gulf.

blocks.caption: Long-range US bombers have operated out of Fairford since it was set up near the end of World War IIImage: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did Rubio and Trump say about the case?

Marco Rubio said in an interview with Fox News that while there was much he could not say on air for now, the security scare during which five young men were detained constituted a very serious situation.

"It's one that clearly involves the hand of a foreign actor. I won't get into great detail about that yet," he said, without mentioning Iran until a later point in the interview in a more hypothetical context.

"I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally," Rubio said.
The Iranian Embassy in London, meanwhile, said that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" of Iranian involvement.
Rubio also echoed President Donald Trump in saying that "a lot of people are disturbed by the news that some of these people have released on bail."
Trump had mentioned the issue in comments to reporters in the White House earlier on Monday.
"I will tell you, I would have said, 'Don't let them have bail.' I'm surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that," he said.
UK releases air base plot suspects
What have British investigators said about the case?

Five men in their 20s, all from the London area and with British citizenship, were arrested on Sunday in the vicinity of the air base, which is in a rural area roughly two hours' drive west of the capital. They were wearing face coverings.
Police seized three "suspicious" white vans and evacuated around 85 households in the vicinity, bringing in bomb disposal teams.

Locals were able to return home on Monday, and preliminary reports from the British Press Association and others suggestd the materials in the vehicles were not viable explosives, but counterterrorism and explosives experts continued to examine the scene.

The head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, acknowledged the "significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident," and said investigators were considering "every possible angle."
One of these angles, he said, was the possibility "that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state."
Taylor said that the men had been released under stringent conditions, and that granting them bail did not in any signify an end to investigations against them.
Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said that decisions like granting bail were operational matters for police and prosecutors, not politicians.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a security meeting known as Cobra, after the secure Cabinet Office Briefing Room A that hosts such sessions, on Monday evening.

blocks.caption: Even prior to Sunday's deployment, security was already tighter than usual at sensitive UK facilities like RAF FairfordImage: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

blocks.text: What is RAF Fairford?
RAF Fairford is a large military airbase not far north of Swindon in Gloucestershire, west of London.

It's a base for US heavy bombers in Europe and has been used as a launch point for operations involving long-range B-52s in a series of conflicts in recent decades including both Iraq wars, the NATO bombing of the former Yugoslavia, and most recently in a limited capacity in Iran this year.
Residents in the Cotswolds region had noted an increased security presence and activity at the base amid the conflict, as is often observable around such bases during such periods.

Because of the longstanding close military ties — and very often infrastructure set up during World War II when Nazi Germany occupied much of Europe — southern England is home to a string of airbases also used by the US military.

articles.title: 1 in 8 cancer cases worldwide are caused by infections, study finds

image.caption: A health worker shows vials of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine during a campaign aiming to protect girls from cervical cancer, in Karachi, Pakistan, in 2025. The virus causes 100 per cent of cases of cervical cancer. (Fareed Khan/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: For many people, sun exposure, smoking and family history are the first thoughts that come to mind regarding cancer risk factors. While infections are rarely high on the list, new research shows one in eight cancers worldwide are actually caused by them.

These viruses, bacteria and other microbes are the focus of a new paper published Monday in The Lancet Oncology that linked an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 — 12 per cent of all new cases — to these infectious agents.

A team of researchers at The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), an arm of the World Health Organization, conducted the study. They found the largest number of cancer cases attributed to infections globally were caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, which can increase the risk of stomach cancer and accounted for 760,000 cases, predominantly in eastern Asia.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) followed close behind. HPV, which causes 100 per cent of cervical cancer cases and also anal, vulvar, vaginal, penile and some head and neck cancers, accounted for nearly 750,000 new cases globally, with high rates in sub-Saharan Africa. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) were also linked to a significant number of liver cancer cases.
For the first time, researchers linked even more cancers to infections, expanding their list to include 16 additional ones.
Gary Clifford, a cancer epidemiologist and study co-author based in Lyon, France, said the science has advanced significantly.

"There's been new infectious agents identified in this time as being cancer-causing, and even the infectious agents that we knew about in the past, the evidence has increased about the number of different cancers that they can cause," he said.
Some of those new infectious agents included HIV and its link to cervical cancer, and a very rare virus called Merkel cell polyomavirus that can lead to an aggressive form of skin cancer.

To come up with numbers, researchers first examined which infections cause cancer, then calculated what fraction of these cancers can be linked to specific infections and applied those calculations to global databases of new cancer cases.

Another significant shift is the recognition of the role of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). EBV was linked to about 260,000 cases globally in 2024, and can lead to nasopharyngeal cancer, some gastric cancers and Hodgkin's lymphoma.
"That's quite a big burden of cancer caused by Epstein-Barr virus that was not counted in the past, but is now recognized," Clifford said.

Epstein-Barr virus is also a key risk factor in developing multiple sclerosis, and unlike some of the other infections that have vaccines or antibiotic treatments, there are no available tools to fight against it.

items: New findings 'strongly suggest' Epstein-Barr virus may help trigger multiple sclerosis

blocks.text: "The fact that we're seeing Epstein-Barr has caused all these chronic diseases — it's increasingly becoming a target that people need to focus on for prevention," he said.

The global report highlights vast regional differences, mostly driven by historical disparities, researchers said. High-income countries that established cancer screening and vaccination programs over the last few decades are doing much better compared to lower- and medium-resourced countries where access to prevention and treatment is limited.
"We really still have a lot of work to do implementing things that we know work and we've known for a long time but haven't really made it into all populations in the world," Clifford said.
In North America, the burden of cancer-causing infections is much lower, but H. pylori and HPV are the most common sources.
Infections causing cancer in Canada

In Canada, according to a 2019 study, the rate of cancers attributable to infections was estimated to be at four per cent. Karena Volesky, an epidemiologist in Montreal, led the Canadian research team while at McGill University.
"It tells us how important each of the 12 infections are," Volesky said of the new global numbers.
While there is a lower prevalence of these forms of infections in Canada, her study estimated these infections lead to more than 7,000 cancer diagnoses each year.
Doctors urge Canadians to get HPV vaccine to prevent cervical cancer
"HPV is certainly an infection that we're keeping an eye on in Canada," said Elizabeth Holmes, the director of health policy at the Canadian Cancer Society.
Holmes said cervical cancer rates had been steadily declining in Canada due to robust childhood vaccination programs, but plateaued last year.
"That's certainly a concern — that we might not meet our goal of elimination of cervical cancer by 2040 unless those rates start to decline again," she said.

items: Cervical cancer rates show a 'concerning plateau,' according to new Canadian Cancer Society data

blocks.text: Human papillomavirus is transmitted through sexual contact, but the HPV vaccine protects against the most common forms of infection that can cause cancer.
Canada's cervical cancer elimination plan aims to increase vaccination rates to 90 per cent, increase screening rates to 90 per cent and ensure timely followup care after screening.
"Right now, only about five provinces are above 80 per cent, and I think at least one is as low as 66 per cent," Holmes said.
The stomach bacteria that can lead to cancer

The infection leading to the most cancer cases is Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium first discovered in the early 1980s that mainly leads to gastric cancers. While the research found the highest burden in eastern Asia in countries like Japan, South Korea and China, it's a problem here, too.
"It's a horrible disease to die from," said Dr. Paul Moayyedi, a leading researcher and gastroenterologist at McMaster University. About 2,000 Canadians die every year from stomach cancer.

Moayyedi wants to see a universal screening program for the bacterium, which can be detected through a blood or breath test, stool sample or endoscopy and treated with a combination of antibiotics over a two-week period.

Helicobacter pylori is associated with crowded living conditions and poor sanitation in childhood. While most people with it can live a long life without any issues, if left untreated, it can cause ulcers and stomach cancer for some.

Moayyedi said stomach cancers may not be seen as high priority compared to other types of cancers, but believes screening programs for those at high risk, such as people with a family history of stomach cancers or First Nations communities, would save lives.
"In consultation with the elders of local communities it would be important to at least offer those groups screening if they would want it," he said.

articles.title: How a rape rumour sent an Indian university into turmoil and emptied hostels
articles.summary: Police are trying to verify whether a female student was raped at Lovely Professional University (LPU).

blocks.text: Image source, Pardeep Sharma/BBC
Some violent protesters allegedly torched police cars parked on the highway on Sunday
ByZoya Mateen & Azadeh Moshiri
BBC News, Delhi
One of India's largest private universities has suspended classes after an unverified allegation that a female student was raped on campus set off protests that descended into violence.

Police say they have registered a case and are trying to verify whether last week's alleged rape at Lovely Professional University (LPU) did happen. The university has categorically denied the allegation.

Police say no student has come forward to say she was assaulted, investigators have yet to identify the alleged victim or the perpetrator, and CCTV footage examined so far has yielded no evidence of an attack.
But rumours on student WhatsApp groups led to unrest over the weekend at the sprawling 600-acre university in Punjab that draws students from India and abroad.

Founded in 2005 by a family whose business began with a small sweet shop, LPU has grown into a largely self-contained world of hostels and lecture halls, with thousands of young people living on campus.

Images and videos showed vehicles in flames, crowds filling a major highway and police wielding canes as unrest spilled beyond the university gates. Police vehicles were damaged, officers injured and parts of the campus was vandalised.
By Monday, the highway had reopened and the campus was calmer, but heavily policed.

University authorities described the claims circulating on social media as false and baseless, but it did little to reassure students with hostels emptying within hours. Key exams were postponed and students were allowed to go home.
Following demands from protesting students, police registered a rape case against "an unidentified person" and formed a seven-member special investigation team, or SIT, to investigate.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Lovely Professional University has suspended classes for 10 days amid violent protests

blocks.text: Lovely Professional University has suspended classes for 10 days amid violent protests
What happened?
The unrest began in the early hours of 27 September, when word spread that a female student had been raped in or near one of the university's hostels a few days earlier.

The suspect was variously described - by students and in media reports - as a plumber, painter or construction worker. Some students said the assault had occurred on 23 September and accused the university of failing to act after being informed.
BBC Punjabi found that messages about the allegation had circulated through WhatsApp groups. As they travelled, crowds gathered.

Hundreds eventually spilled on to National Highway 44, a major route between Delhi and Punjab, blocking traffic for more than 15 hours. By Sunday evening, university property had been damaged, objects set alight and stones thrown at police vehicles. Videos showed police striking protesters with canes, although police later denied carrying out a baton-charge.
Behind the gates, students described a night of fear.

"We were sitting with knives and scissors," Arya, a student, told BBC Punjabi. Students had been told to lock themselves inside their rooms, she said, while people knocked on their doors. "We were just thinking that somehow this night would pass and we would get out of here."
Police later arrived and made them feel safer, she said. By the next day, she wanted to leave. "Our parents also want us to just get out of here."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Arya, a student at the college, says they thought about nothing but leaving the campus on the night of violence

blocks.text: Image source, BBC Punjabi
Arya, a student at the college, says they thought about nothing but leaving the campus on the night of violence
So why have police lodged a case?
Because that was among the protesters' central demands.

"The students have been demanding that an FIR [First Information Report] is to be registered, but the students could not provide us with any victim's name," senior police official Naveen Singla told the BBC.
Police nevertheless registered an FIR under India's rape law against an unidentified person. An FIR formally records an allegation for investigation; it does not establish that a crime occurred.
Singla said investigators had also begun examining CCTV footage. The preliminary search, he told the BBC, had so far shown no outsider entering a room.
"As of now, it can't be verified that rape has happened or not," he said.
But they are continuing to examine the footage.

"The campus is quite large, so we haven't been able to see all the cameras yet," Sinha told reporters on Monday. "We have initially checked the places that the students had mentioned, but we will get to the bottom of this."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesting students had earlier blocked a nearby highway which was opened later on Monday

blocks.text: Protesting students had earlier blocked a nearby highway which was opened later on Monday
Why did the protests grow so large?
It is difficult to say. What began with an allegation of rape quickly became a broader protest over security, the university's response and, eventually, the violence itself.

There was also growing uncertainty over who was on the campus. Some students insisted the demonstrations had begun peacefully and blamed outsiders for at least some of the violence. Others told BBC Punjabi of seeing masked or unfamiliar people inside the university.
"We were really scared," said Pawan, a student. "It became a complete battlefield."

Another student, Aniket Singh, said outsiders had entered a women's hostel and knocked on doors claiming to be police officers. Police have since confirmed that outsiders were among the crowds, but said they were still trying to establish who they were and what role they played.
Amid that confusion, the university's attempt to dispel the rape allegation produced a controversy of its own.
On Monday, LPU released a video of three women living in the hostel room that had been linked to the alleged assault. They said nothing had happened there and asked people to stop disturbing them.

The same students later alleged in another video that university officials had instructed them what to say, edited the recording and posted it without their consent. Those claims have not been independently verified. LPU has not commented on the students' allegations.

Another claim circulating during the protests sought to connect the alleged rape with the recent suicide of a female LPU student from Telangana state. Police say investigations into her death had already begun and there is no verified evidence linking the two cases.

blocks.caption: Image caption, There is heavy police presence around the university campus since the unrest

blocks.text: Image source, ANI
There is heavy police presence around the university campus since the unrest
What is happening now?
For now, life on campus has been interrupted. Regular classes have been suspended for 10 days and exams postponed. Students have been asked to return home after consulting their parents or guardians.
Those who are staying have been advised to stay in their residences and avoid further unrest.
The Punjab State Women's Commission has also sought the FIR, details of the investigation and information about arrangements for students' safety.
The investigation now has two separate questions to answer: whether there is evidence of the assault that set the protests in motion? And who was responsible for the violence that followed?

Addressing the students on Monday, LPU's pro-chancellor Rashmi Mittal said she was hurt that despite the university's many channels for students to raise concerns, they had instead "believed the rumour that was spreading". She also alleged that outsiders had joined the unrest.
"I feel students can't do this," she said.
Additional reporting by Harmandeep Singh, BBC Punjabi

articles.title: PNP probes cop over alleged social media post on Sara Duterte impeachment
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Tuesday said it is investigating a police corporal assigned in Region 13 over an alleged social media post concerning the impeachment of Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 4:12pm

The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Tuesday said it is investigating a police corporal assigned in Region 13 over an alleged social media post concerning the impeachment of Vice President Sara Duterte.

At a press briefing, PNP spokesperson Police Colonel Allen Rae Co said authorities first need to verify whether the police officer himself made the said post or whether someone else used his name or account.
“If it will be proven that he was the one who posted this, this is a direct violation and a clear violation of our code of conduct and ethical standards,” Co said.
Based on the presentation of the PNP, the police officer posted, “Kung ganyan man lang kadali baguhin ang ating Constitution, I tell you sobrang kawawa natin mga Pilipino.”
(If it were that easy to change our Constitution, I tell you, we Filipinos are so pitiful.)
According to the PNP, the corporal was reacting to the voting threshold in the ongoing impeachment trial of Duterte.
Co said police officers are subject to restrictions on political expression because they are expected to remain politically neutral while performing their duties.
The PNP said that if the corporal is confirmed to have made the post, the matter may be referred to the police disciplinary system for assessment.
Co said possible sanctions would depend on the findings of the investigation and the applicable rules. Dismissal from service was mentioned as one possible sanction.
The PNP said the cop is currently undergoing schooling in Cavite. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Hurricane Polo makes landfall on Mexico's Pacific coast
articles.summary: The storm moved ashore on the Baja California peninsula, which is a popular tourist destination.

blocks.text: Hurricane Polo has made landfall along the northern Pacific coast of Mexico, lashing the state of Baja California Sur with life-threatening winds and heavy rain that has already flooded some coastal areas.
Mexican officials said Polo moved ashore just south of the surfing and fishing village of Las Barrancas bringing maximum sustained winds of 110 mph (175 km/h).

Polo is moving northeast and on the forecast track, its core is predicted to continue passing over Baja California Sur before moving inland over the southern part of the Mexican state of Sonora later on Tuesday.
Residents in threatened areas have been encouraged to seek shelter.
Shopkeeper Maria Palomino, 57, spent the night at a high school which has been turned into a temporary shelter. "If something happens, it's better to come to the shelter," she told AFP news agency.
A whale-watching and fishing guide who was boarding up the facade of his home told AFP the storm was "coming with full force".

The US-based National Hurricane Center (NHC) said that while Polo was expected to weaken as it moved over the Baja California peninsula, it was forecast to still be at hurricane strength when it makes its second landfall in mainland Mexico.

Meteorologists said Polo could dump between 6 and 12 inches (150-300mm) of rain across parts of Baja California Sur, which they warned could produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain.

The NHC said a storm surge was also expected to produce significant coastal flooding in areas of onshore winds. "Near the coast, the surge will be accompanied by large and destructive waves," it said in an update.
Even before Polo made landfall, residents said there were power cuts in Baja California Sur.

US media reported some flooding in the fishing town of Puerto San Carlos and the Associated Press said waves crested sea barriers in the area, where many residents had been evacuated due to the threat.

articles.title: Burkina Faso's junta leader opens major gold refinery to keep mining profits at home
articles.summary: Junta leader Ibrahim Traoré wants the country to profit more from its mineral wealth.

blocks.text: With gold production on the rise, Traoré's government set up a state-owned mining company two years ago.
Foreign mining firms are now required to give the state a 15% stake in their operations and train local workers.
The World Gold Council said output rose by 17% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, helped by increased production at several mines.

But successive governments have struggled to regulate the country's extensive artisanal and small-scale mining industry, where smuggling and informal trading have made it difficult for the authorities to account for all the gold produced.
The government has also alleged that some illegally traded gold helps finance the Islamist insurgency that has engulfed much of the country.
Burkina Faso has been fighting armed Islamist groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State for years, with large areas outside full government control.
The new refinery, known as Raffinor-BF, cost more than 11bn CFA francs ($19m; £14m), according to the presidency.
It said the project was financed by the state, including through the National Precious Metals Company (Sonasp), in partnership with Burkina Faso's private sector.
The plant will initially be capable of refining 164 tonnes of gold a year, significantly more than the country's current annual production.
The government says its eventual capacity could rise to 515 tonnes, suggesting it also wants the refinery to process gold from elsewhere in the region.
"This is the day we take back the keys to our own house," Mines Minister Yacouba Zabré Gouba said at the opening.
"Our gold will no longer be used to create added value for others while our people remain in need."

The refinery is the latest element of Capt Traoré's drive to increase state control over Burkina Faso's natural resources and reduce its economic dependence on foreign companies and former Western partners.
Since taking power in a coup in September 2022, the 38-year-old army captain has promoted a nationalist economic agenda centred on domestic production and greater control of strategic industries.
His government has increased state involvement in the mining sector and has sought to reorganise the trade in artisanal gold.
The authorities suspended exports of gold produced by artisanal and semi-mechanised mines in 2024, saying the move was intended to better regulate the sector.
Capt Traoré has previously accused smugglers of taking large quantities of gold out of Burkina Faso illegally and said some of the proceeds were helping finance militant groups.
The refinery also forms part of a broader government campaign to process more commodities domestically rather than exporting them in raw form.
Traoré has presented such projects as evidence of Burkina Faso becoming more economically self-reliant, alongside investments in industries including cotton, textiles and food processing.

His policies have coincided with historically high international gold prices and increased global production. Worldwide mine output reached an estimated record 3,672 tonnes in 2025, according to the World Gold Council.
Burkina Faso's government says the new plant should eventually be capable of refining all the gold produced by both its industrial mines and artisanal miners.
Several West African countries are also seeking to process more of their gold at home.
Guinea and Ghana have restricted exports of unrefined gold, while Mali is building its first refinery with help of a Russian firm. Ivory Coast also plans to open a refinery next year.

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial recap, Sept. 29: Baste Duterte on the stand
articles.summary: Davao City Mayor Baste Duterte testified at the impeachment trial of his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, on Tuesday, September 29, saying he had no direct knowledge of the city's 19 contracts…

blocks.text: September 29, 2026 | 4:00pm

MANILA, Philippines — Davao City Mayor Baste Duterte testified at the impeachment trial of his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, on Tuesday, September 29, saying he had no direct knowledge of the city's 19 contracts with a firm declared as a business interest in her SALN.

The direct and cross-examination of the vice president's brother came down to one main question on GenCorp Industries Inc.: Was there a conflict of interest when the Davao City government awarded it contracts, all while his sister was vice president?

On that question, the mayor repeatedly told the court he could only answer based on the record, as he had not personally reviewed contracts with the firm. Baste said it was the city's bids and awards committee that evaluated GenCorp and that an aide signed the contracts under delegated authority.
He said he was not aware of his sister's business interests because, in his words, "we simply do not discuss this."

A hypothetical, however, surfaced during the proceedings, when Presiding Officer Sen. Chiz Escudero asked whether the mayor would have allowed any award to GenCorp had he known his sister was a stockholder.
"I would not allow it," Baste said.

From 2022 to 2026, Davao City awarded GenCorp 19 food and catering contracts, 15 of them through small value procurement, which does not require public bidding. None were entered into while the vice president herself was the city's mayor.

GenCorp's ties to the vice president exist only on her statement of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN), which lists her as a stockholder. The corporate records of the company, however, as the Securities and Exchange Commission has shared with the court, do not list Duterte as such.
Escudero said on Monday that this discrepancy has yet to be reconciled.
Here are the three highlights from today's proceedings.
1. No knowledge of GenCorp, but a business partner of a GenCorp stockholder
Under direct questioning by prosecution counsel Theodore Te, the Davao mayor testified he had no personal knowledge of GenCorp before the company was brought up in the impeachment trial.
The mayor however also confirmed that Jaime T. Cruz, GenCorp's major stockholder, is his business partner in another company whose 2026 corporate filing also lists his brother Paolo Duterte.
Duterte said he never discussed GenCorp with Cruz and did not know of Cruz's stake in it.
Sen. Risa Hontiveros asked Baste to describe Cruz's relationship with the Dutertes.
"Maybe not entirely the family, but he's a friend of my father. He's a known businessman in Davao," the mayor said.
Hontiveros said that made the relationship a "close" one.
2. "The witness is not the one on trial"
Escudero repeatedly pressed prosecutors to connect their questions to the article at hand, as "the witness is not the one on trial here."
Sens. Alan Peter Cayetano, JV Ejercito, Bong Go and Joel Villanueva used their turns to argue that a mayor cannot check every single document he signs.
Sen. Ping Lacson noted that the mayor "never denied anything" and asked whether his lawyers had told him of the Arias doctrine, which lets office heads rely on subordinates in good faith.
Sen. Erwin Tulfo asked whether the mayor would look into the contracts himself.
That produced a non-committal answer from the vice president's brother.
"Well, as long as my sister's name, the vice president's name was not on the contract then there's nothing," Baste replied.
3. No answer required
Escudero announced today the court's ruling on the prosecution's request for admission on some 104 items pertaining to her and her husband's bank and tax records.
The court sided with the defense and ruled Duterte does not have to answer the prosecution's 104-item request for admission, citing her right against self-incrimination.
"The prosecution cannot shift its burden of proof to respondent through the simple expedience of a request for admission," Escudero said.
Escudero also declined to subpoena former Sen. Antonio Trillanes, whom prosecutors wanted to advance as their first witness tomorrow.

Escudero expressed his reluctance and said the prosecution's own motion tied Trillanes's testimony to bank records that have not yet been presented: "The cart cannot be put ahead of the horse," he said.
However, the presiding officer also told the prosecution nothing stopped it from voluntarily calling Trillanes as a witness this week without a subppoena.
The former senator was in the gallery today during Baste's presentation.

articles.title: Grave of boy who vanished at residential school found decades later, First Nation looks for others like him
articles.summary: The family of 11-year-old Johnny Kiyawasew, who never came home from St. Francis Xavier residential school, spent decades searching for answers. Now, Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation and the University of…

image.caption: Robert Kiyawasew's brother Johnny Kiyawasew was 11 years old in 1943 when he didn't return from St. Francis Xavier residential school in Calais, Alta. (Justin Pennell)

blocks.text: Indigenous

The family of 11-year-old Johnny Kiyawasew, who never came home from St. Francis Xavier residential school, spent decades searching for answers. Now, Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation and the University of Alberta say they're doing extensive research to uncover the stories of other children like Johnny who went to residential school but never made it home.
'It's not right… the church should have told my dad that he had passed away,' says brother
Johnny Kiyawasew was 11 years old when he died in a small town hospital in northern Alberta in 1943, a world away from his Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation family.
Forced to enroll at Catholic-run St. Francis Xavier Residential School in Calais, Alta., Johnny never returned home, and it was decades before his brothers and sisters learned what happened to him.
"My parents, like my dad, was never told about nothing. They wrote a death certificate without his knowledge or nothing," said Robert Kiyawasew, Johnny's younger brother.
"It's not right… the church should have told my dad that he had passed away."
After years of unanswered questions, Robert Kiyawasew said his older sister Roseann, with the help of a private investigator, found Johnny's gravesite in 2013.
"That caretaker said, 'I know exactly where he's buried and I'll show you where,'" said Robert Kiyawasew.
According to provincial records, Johnny died of pulmonary tuberculosis in a hospital in High Prairie, where he is buried, over 75 kilometres away from the residential school.

Now, Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation and the University of Alberta say they're undergoing extensive research to uncover the stories of children like Johnny, including many of his relatives, who went to residential school but never made it home.
'It is heartbreaking'
Sheldon Sunshine, chief of Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation, said research shows many children enrolled at St. Francis Xavier died from tuberculosis and malnutrition.
"It's not data, it's people," said Sunshine.

"When you see the names and, you know, it's saddening, what our people went through, having perished because of the results of the living conditions in that school, having perished because of the results of the living conditions in that school. It is heartbreaking."
Robert Kiyawasew said he's thankful his sister was able to track down Johnny's grave before she died.
"I visit every time I have a chance now," said Robert Kiyawasew.
"To see that lonely little grave, out there all alone."
Sturgeon Lake family's search for a brother lost at residential school
A day school survivor himself, Robert Kiyawasew said he experienced harms similar to his siblings who attended St. Francis Xavier, and was punished for speaking his language.
"To treat us Natives like we don't exist… no," said Robert Kiyawasew.
"We belong in our culture. Our heritage is our right to be like that."

items: After 50-year search, Inuk mother finds daughter's grave 2,000 km from home
Letitia John died at a residential school. Her identity was lost until now

blocks.text: According to the Sturgeon Lake residential school narrative at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation (NCTR), a summary of the school's history prepared by the Government of Canada as part of its response to litigation, at least five children died at the school in 1943.

It quotes a 1943 document saying the school "is falling to ruin and has become a source of danger for the health of Indian children as well as a fire hazard," adding some student deaths "last winter" had been said to be due to "the lack of comfort" resulting from poor heating.
Difficulty obtaining records
Raymond Frogner, senior director of research and head of archives at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, said residential school records were disorganized, inconsistent and unreliable.
"It was managed by church groups, which are private, provincial governments, federal governments, and all of these organizations never talked to each other," said Frogner.
"It's like putting a jigsaw puzzle back together when the pieces are missing."
Frogner said many church records are not available, have incorrect or different dates from provincial or federal documents, and when they are tracked down they are often withheld.
Sunshine said several times Sturgeon Lake researchers have been told by church officials they will only release the documents of a student to someone with family ties.

items: Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation says 62 potential unmarked graves found on northern Alberta reserve

blocks.text: "How do you have family ties when a lot of them are passing away?" said Sunshine.
"That really shuts the door on finding that information…. It's going to limit us to finding all of our children."
Sunshine said the First Nation will continue to work to piece together the stories of children who were enrolled at St. Francis Xavier and never came home.
"If we don't know where these children are, how can we find closure for some of our families?" said Sunshine.
"Talking about intergenerational trauma? That's part of it."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Edzi'u Loverin is a graduate of CBC's Indigenous Pathways Program and has reported in Vancouver and Winnipeg since 2024. Edzi'u is a member of the Taku River Tlingit First Nation and a registered member of the Tahltan Nation, but is currently based in xʷməθkʷəy̓əm, Sḵwx̱wú7mesh, and səlilwətaɬ territories. articles.title: ShinyHunters hackers say they won't leak sensitive FBI data
articles.summary: The hacking group behind a massive FBI data breach says it will not publish the information it obtained, but it cannot guarantee what will happen with the data it already shared with journalists.

image.caption: ShinyHunters told CBC News they achieved their goals with a massive FBI data breach and do not intend to release the information to the public. (Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New
The hacking group behind a massive FBI data breach says it will not publish the information it obtained, but it cannot guarantee what will happen with the data it already shared with journalists.
A representative added, however, that data they already shared is 'out of our control'
The hacking group behind a massive FBI data breach says it will not publish the information it obtained, but cannot guarantee what will happen with the data it already shared.

ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for stealing a massive trove of data from the FBI last Tuesday — including officials' job assignments, addresses and social security numbers — and gave the law enforcement agency one week to rescind an ⁠unflattering statement about the group.

With the deadline approaching, a ShinyHunters representative sent CBC News a statement Monday saying they were never planning to release the sensitive data, adding that the media and the public have "made many false assumptions and wild speculations."

The group has been linked to dozens of cyberattacks targeting large companies and institutions. ShinyHunters typically demand ransom payments in exchange for not releasing sensitive data, but they have been adamant that was not their intention in this case.
Campaign to 'combat disinformation'
ShinyHunters denied asking the FBI for a ransom, but acknowledged "past operations" could leave them open to misinterpretation.

"The reason why we have stated multiple times that this is not extortion is because since the very beginning we had made our decision that we would never publish this data. We have never intended to nor have we ever planned to," the statement said in part.
The group told CBC News that their actions against the FBI were part of a campaign to "combat disinformation" about their tactics.

"If we made this statement normally then this much attention to our words and intentions would've never been this widespread. We'd have been ignored and disregarded. However, now everyone knows what the issue is and what we are doing."

ShinyHunters took issue with an FBI report from May that said, among other things, the group is known to threaten family members of its targets and threaten to release embarrassing or compromising images of its victims.

items: What drives ShinyHunters, the group that claimed responsibility for hacking the FBI?
Dutch police arrest security professional in ShinyHunters investigation

blocks.text: ShinyHunters denied ever using those tactics and released a statement following last Tuesday's data breach giving the FBI one week to remove or "correct" the report.
The group shared a 5,000-line spreadsheet of breached FBI data with some journalists, which it said represented only a small piece of its claimed two- to three-terabyte trove.
The sample included names, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, social security numbers and emergency contact details for what it claimed were thousands of FBI employees.

When CBC News asked ShinyHunters on Monday whether they have taken any steps to ensure the shared data isn't leaked by other sources, the representative said they "cannot guarantee" what will happen to those samples, "because that is out of our control and certain journalists violated our trust."
There's a data breach at Canadian schools. What do we know?
'Can't trust them,' researcher says
Ian Lin, an ethical hacker and head of research and development at Toronto-based cybersecurity company Packetlabs, says that's concerning.
He says he's seen "a number of researchers" claiming online to have obtained the data, in addition to journalists.
"There's going to be people that are willing to pay a high price for this data," Lin told CBC News.

items: A cyberattack hit universities worldwide, including top Canadian schools. Here's what we know
Telus probes cybersecurity incident that 'ShinyHunters' group claims responsibility for

blocks.text: The hack, which one former FBI operative called a "foreign intelligence service goldmine," has raised concerns about the safety of the agency's employees.

The New York Times reported Monday that the FBI sent out a staff memo acknowledging employees had personal information stolen in a cybersecurity incident, and instructing them to remain vigilant at home and at work and report any unsolicited contacts or threats.

Lin says he does not have high hopes ShinyHunters will keep their word, saying it's common for criminal hacking groups to renege on their promises or to use the same set of data as leverage multiple times.

"Why they did this, I think was for attention. But you still can't trust them to keep safe your data. Because now this is leverage over the law enforcement and FBI. And at any moment they could choose to use this data for their own additional purposes," he said.
"The FBI and law enforcement should all still remain vigilant. There should be massive lessons learned from the FBI side."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kevin Maimann is a senior writer for CBC News based in Edmonton. He has covered a wide range of topics for publications including VICE, the Toronto Star, Xtra Magazine and the Edmonton Journal. You can reach Kevin by email at kevin.maimann@cbc.ca.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Why Montreal’s most iconic landmark will fade from the city skyline for 1 year
articles.summary: In total, about one quarter of the cross's 1,800 steel parts will be replaced. Its outdated lighting system will also be swapped out.

image.caption: The cross on Montreal's Mount Royal 'goes deep into our psyche and is part of our identity, it is a unifying force,' says Alan DeSousa. (Natalia Weichsel/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal·Updated
In total, about one quarter of the cross's 1,800 steel parts will be replaced. Its outdated lighting system will also be swapped out.
Work on the Mount Royal landmark will force off the cross's illumination
Why Montreal’s most iconic landmark will fade from the city skyline for 1 year
Montreal’s landmark cross will have its lights turned off Tuesday.
The well-known steel structure — which weighs 26 metric tons and sits at the top of Mount Royal — is easily visible against the night sky thanks to its 240 lightbulbs.

The cross is about as tall as a 10-storey building, says Jean Carrier, director of the City of Montreal’s road infrastructure department, "so it's a huge infrastructure we can see from everywhere in Montreal."
It will be unplugged to allow for repairs, expected to cost the City of Montreal $3.7 million, according to Carrier.

The updates, which are expected to take a year, will address non-urgent corrosion to the cross’s central portion, ensure it meets current building standards and reinforce it against harsh weather conditions.
In total, about one quarter of the landmark’s 1,800 steel parts will be replaced. Its outdated lighting system will also be swapped out.
The work will be done in phases with breaks, to avoid disturbing the nesting periods of birds and other wildlife in the area.
The project is expected to conclude by next fall, at which time the cross will once again be set aglow.
Can a cross be a secular symbol?
Even though the cross is a religious symbol, it gets a pass under Quebec’s secularism laws, according to Pearl Eliadis, a human rights lawyer and law professor at McGill University.
"The characterization of the cross is that it is essentially a cultural relic, if you will, or a historical element," said Eliadis. "I think people do see a degree of hypocrisy in that."
The current one was erected in 1924, but a cross has stood in the spot ever since 1642, the year Montreal was founded.
"The cross is part of our heritage," said Alan DeSousa, a member of the City of Montreal's executive committee, which is responsible for the maintenance of infrastructure.
"It goes deep into our psyche and is part of our identity, it is a unifying force," he said.
DeSousa says the city has not just a legal, but also moral responsibility to protect monuments that speak to Montreal’s identity.
"People are very sensitive to the preservation of this park and the cross, because it's part of who they are," said DeSousa. "They want to maintain their traditions."

Eliadis notes that the cross's presence on the mountain likely isn’t a priority for minority religious groups affected by Law 9's increased focus on promoting secularism, which included restrictions such as the prohibition of public prayer and an extension of the ban on religious symbols to daycare staff.

items: With secularism sidelined in Quebec election campaign, here's where the parties stand
How public institutions — like schools and the STM — are handling Quebec's new secularism law

blocks.text: "I think most people can live with the cross on the mountain," she said. "Very few people I know have gone to the battlefield on this."
However, she says, it is important to remember that Law 9 has attempted to remove religion from public spaces in Quebec.
“If you are going to have secularism as your most important social value … then as I say, there does seem to be a degree of lack of coherence," she said.
Corrections
