articles.title: Rights group accuses Vietnam of abducting Australian and Norwegian activists
articles.summary: Vietnam says the men entered the country illegally and accused them of planning terrorist activities.

blocks.text: A pro-democracy group has accused the Vietnamese government of abducting two of its members, an Australian and a Norwegian citizen, in Cambodia and taking them back across the border.
Vietnamese authorities confirmed that they had arrested Tran Hiep and Nguyen Duc Thuan, but say they had entered the country using forged documents and planned to carry out terrorist activities.
It said the men had admitted to being members of Viet Tan, which Vietnam sees as a terrorist organisation.
Viet Tan called their arrest a "blatant fabrication intended to conceal the fact that the Viet Tan members were abducted in Cambodia and forcibly taken to Vietnam".

The group, which has members in Vietnam and abroad, said the two men had been travelling in the southern border district of Kaoh Andaet in Cambodia when they went missing and had not been heard from since 18 September.
Tran's wife, Chloe Dang, told Australian media he had been meeting pro-democracy activists in Cambodia and had no intention of travelling to Vietnam.
He was meant to meet her in Bangkok to board a return flight to Australia but never turned up, she said.
"He always knew there was a risk doing human rights work, but we never thought that this would happen," she told the ABC.
According to a Vietnamese state media report published on Monday, Tran and Nguyen were detained with a third man at the border in Tay Ninh province on 18 September.

The trio "confessed to being members of the terrorist organisation 'Viet Tan,' [and] carrying forged documents to illegally enter Vietnam in order to carry out terrorist and sabotage activities," the report said.

They were charged on Monday with membership of a terrorist organisation while an investigation continued "to clarify the criminal acts of the suspects in order to handle them according to the law", it said.

"A state orchestrating the abduction of individuals abroad and forcibly taking them to its territory is a serious act of transnational repression," said Viet Tan. "It violates Cambodia's sovereignty and the fundamental principles of international law."
The Viet Tan statement did not mention the third man, who was named by authorities as Thai Cong Truong Son.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said consular support was being provided to Tran's family.
"That's what Australian governments do for our citizens. And we'll continue to engage directly with the family."

"Vietnam authorities' confirmation that they detained [these] activists... demonstrates yet again that Hanoi is arguably the most vicious and pernicious practitioner of transnational repression today in Southeast Asia," Phil Robertson, Director of Asia Human Rights and Labor Advocates said in a statement.
"This latest act is an unacceptable outrage."
The Vietnamese and Cambodian authorities have been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Palestinian embassy thanks Philippines for joining UN walkout on Netanyahu
articles.summary: The Palestinian embassy in Manila on Monday, September 28, thanked the Philippine government for joining last week's walkout on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the United Nations, an…

blocks.text: September 29, 2026 | 12:23pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Palestinian embassy in Manila on Monday, September 28, thanked the Philippine government for joining last week's walkout on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the United Nations, an action it says demonstrated Manila's "principled position."

The walkout placed the Philippines, which has kept close relations with Israel for decades, among the dozens of delegations that exited the General Assembly hall as Netanyahu took the podium on September 24.

The Department of Foreign Affairs confirmed Manila's participation to Philstar.com on Sunday, after independent tallies of the protest, many drawn from video clips of the proceedings, had listed the Philippines among the countries that stayed back in the hall.

In its statement, the Embassy of the State of Palestine said it "expresses its sincere appreciation" to the government and the DFA for the delegation's stance at the assembly's 81st session, "including its participation in the walkout."

The embassy also welcomed the Philippines' "expressed concern over the grave humanitarian situation in Gaza, the advancement of the E1 settlement plan, and the continuing rise of settler violence in the West Bank."

"This position reflects the Philippines' commitment to international law, peace, and the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people," the embassy said. It also cited Palestinians' right to self-determination and Manila's support for a two-state solution.

Manila said it joined the walkout as a call for peace directed at all sides. DFA Spokesperson Analyn Ratonel told Philstar.com that the delegation walked out "in global solidarity for peace in the Middle East" and to urge all parties to stop unilateral actions that erode the conditions for peace.

Ratonel cited Israel's push to advance the E1 plan, along with rising settler violence in the West Bank, as "detrimental to finding a just, lasting and comprehensive solution to the Middle East conflict."
When asked about the walkout on Monday at a briefing, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro repeated the DFA's explanation.
'Consistent and principled'
Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro expressed the same calls for peace in her own speech to the General Assembly on Saturday, September 26.

"We reiterate our call for an immediate and sustained ceasefire in Gaza," Lazaro said. She reaffirmed Manila's "consistent and principled support for the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people."
The Philippines–Palestine Friendship Association, a Manila-based group, also welcomed the walkout.
The group said solidarity with Palestinians had never been more important, citing what it called Israel's "continuing genocide, occupation, and war crimes."

"This is proof that governments can no longer afford to be passive spectators. The times demand that the international community stand on the side of humanity, justice, and the Palestinian people's right to self-determination," the group said in a statement.
This was the third straight year that Netanyahu's General Assembly address drew a walkout.
After briefly pausing at the sight of delegates streaming toward the exit, Netanyahu opened his speech by telling any "moral cowards" still in their seats to leave.

In a September 17 statement, the DFA had already flagged E1 and settler violence, warning that both "may contravene international law." That statement came about a month after Israel opened bids for over 1,000 housing units in E1.
Dozens of countries have warned that the project would split the West Bank and break up Palestinian territory.

Settler attacks, demolitions and evictions forced more Palestinians from their homes from January to April 2026 than in the whole of 2025, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

articles.title: US ban on Canadian alcohol and dairy comes into effect as trade war drags on
articles.summary: It is the latest escalation in the Canada-US trade war after negotiations collapsed in late August, with no word on when talks may resume.

blocks.text: A US ban on several Canadian imports, including alcohol, dairy and motorcycles, has come into effect as a trade war between the two neighbours drags on.
The latest measure by the Trump administration is in response to Canada's implementation of tariffs on a range of US goods earlier this month following a breakdown in trade talks.
Canada is not expected to retaliate further, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying earlier this month that the impact the import bans will have on Canada's economy is "modest".
Trade talks remain on ice, with US trade representative Jamieson Greer telling CNBC recently that President Donald Trump is "comfortable" with his current relationship with Canada.

"They call us now and then and we have good conversations about potential deals. But there's no urgency on our side," Greer said of relations with Canada in an interview with the US network last week.
Tuesday's trade ban applies to nearly C$1bn ($710m; £530m) worth of Canadian liquor exported to the US, as well as whey products used in protein powder.

Motorcycle exports to the US will also be impacted, though Canada only sent about 5,000 motorcycles south of the border in 2025 that were worth about C$120m, according to national data by Statistics Canada, meaning the impact would be limited.

The import bans were first announced by Trump in a series of executive orders signed on 8 September. In them, Trump said the measures are in response to "continued discrimination" by Canada on US dairy, automotives and alcohol.
Speaking to reports on Monday, he accused Canada of "treating the United States very unfairly".
"They have been one of the worst countries in the entire world," Trump said.
Carney said earlier this month that the bans "are relatively modest measures" when compared to other trade actions the US has imposed on Canada.
He acknowledged, however, that the bans will hurt certain businesses and sectors that are directly targeted.
Derek Holt, an economist with Canadian bank Scotiabank, wrote in an analysis that "these actions are face-saving by the US administration, not substantive in nature and that's a positive".

About 93% of all Canadian liquor exports in 2025 were sold to the US. Spirits Canada, a group representing Canadian liquor producers, has said the consequences to the industry "could be significant"., external
Economists and businesses have also warned that the bans will add uncertainty to the future of Canada's trade relationship with the US, its largest trade partner.

In addition to these latest import bans, the US has imposed 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, including dairy, alcohol, steel and aluminium products, as well as 25% tariffs on Canadian-built cars.

Canada in return has placed retaliatory tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on more than 700 US products, as well as a 25% levy on certain steel and aluminium products. Most Canadian provinces have also stopped selling US liquor.
Tariffs - taxes paid on imported goods - are central to Trump's economic agenda, who argues that they raise government revenue and encourage consumers to buy American-made goods.
Economists, however, argue that they have raised prices of everyday goods for consumers and have disrupted the global economy.

articles.title: Argentina threatens legal action against UK over Falkland Islands oil exploration
articles.summary: President Javier Milei set a two-week deadline for the Sea Lion oilfield project to be scrapped.

blocks.text: Argentina's president has threatened to launch a legal challenge against the British government unless it halts oil exploration work off the coast of the Falkland Islands.
In a social media post, President Javier Milei set a two-week deadline for the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between Israeli and British companies, to be scrapped.
The companies insist they have valid licences issued by Britain.

The comments heighten tensions between the UK and Argentina over the sovereignty of the archipelago, known in Argentina as Las Malvinas, more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982.

Milei said that if the two-week deadline was not met, he had "instructed the Foreign Ministry and legal teams to initiate international arbitration" against the UK over what he called "the illegal plundering of our resources through the Sea Lion Project".

He continued to warn the UK that if the "illegitimate exploitation" of the region didn't end within two weeks, Argentina would take the matter before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea.
The International Tribunal is an independent judicial body based in Hamburg which is responsible for the fair application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The move comes soon after Milei roundly criticised the UN in his speech at the General Assembly for failing to act over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.
He said the UN had become "a useless organisation" which only serves "arrogant parasites dressed up as well-intentioned bureaucrats".
Since then, the UK Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, said that Argentina "lacks the ability" to take back the Falklands by force.

articles.title: OpenAI shelves new AI model amid safety concerns
articles.summary: The decision comes amid a broader push within the industry to slow the development of increasingly powerful and autonomous systems until safety measures can catch up.

image.caption: OpenAI and other AI companies are facing growing pressure to strengthen safeguards around increasingly autonomous modelsImage: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence company OpenAI has abandoned plans to release a next-generation AI model after internal testing found that the system failed to meet the company's safety and alignment standards.

GPT-6.1 Astra, which is designed to handle increasingly complex tasks with less human intervention, had been scheduled to debut in October but tests reportedly found that the model displayed higher levels of deceptive behavior than its predecessors.

Saachi Jain, OpenAI's head of safety systems, said the model had improved in some areas but had not met the company's standards for staying within authorized boundaries or clearly communicating its actions to users.

"We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users," Jain said. "But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms ⁠of safety and ​alignment."
Pressure builds for stronger AI oversight
The postponement comes as OpenAI and other AI companies face growing pressure to strengthen safeguards around increasingly powerful and autonomous models.
Some of these models developed by OpenAI and rival lab Anthropic have been involved in security incidents during testing.

Earlier this month, OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman and Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei joined other industry leaders in calling for a slower pace of AI development and stronger safety measures.
Leading AI executives are set to meet with US President Donald Trump in Washington on Tuesday to discuss the need for finding a balance between AI innovation and oversight.
OpenAI pledges to rebuild trust after government website hack
On Tuesday, OpenAI admitted that its models had even accessed Australian government websites and systems without authorization as part of internal training and evaluation exercises in June.

The company said ‌the activity ‌involved ​websites and systems linked to Services Australia, ​the NSW Bureau of ⁠Crime ​Statistics and Research, ​the Victorian ​Department of ‌Health and the Australian ​Institute ⁠of Health and ⁠Welfare.
The incursion, which occurred in June, was not made public until last week.
In a blog post, the ChatGPT maker apologized for the hacking and acknowledged it ‌mishandled its response ⁠and ⁠pledged to take accountability to "rebuild trust with the Australian people."

articles.title: France: Student protests over conditions at French high schools fuel political clashes
articles.summary: Over 160 people were arrested and dozens injured after student protests in France descended into violence. With a presidential election approaching, senior politicians are pointing fingers at each…

image.caption: The student protests began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but on Monday spread to other regionsImage: CLPRESS/abaca/picture alliance

blocks.text: Student protests spread to high schools across France on Monday, resulting in dozens of injuries, over 160 arrests and arguments between senior politicians — a day ahead of a nationwide strike by public sector workers and seven months ahead of the presidential election.

Teenagers at French lycées (equivalent to US high schools) have been blockading their schools since last week in protest at overcrowded classes, heavy workloads, poor quality learning materials and teacher shortages.
The movement began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but on Monday spread to other regions including Lille in the north, Marseille in the south and Sedan in the east.
Video footage on French media showed student protesters lighting flares and firing fireworks, even inside a school building, while police officers responded with tear gas.

blocks.caption: Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the 'escalation' of the situation 'irresponsible'Image: Adnan Farzat/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: French student protests: what have politicians said?
As of Monday night, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez reported incidents at around 180 establishments resulting in 164 arrests and injuries to 12 students, three teachers and 12 police officers.
He acknowledged that the "difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed" but said: "This wasn't about making demands, it was really violence in its purest form."
He added that "a number of individuals … were masked, equipped with fireworks in tubes and projectiles [and] clearly wanted to confront the internal security forces."

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the "escalation" of the situation "irresponsible" and said: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers."
'Hands off our youth!' French politicians clash over protests

Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that the protests, which he described as a "classic high school student movement," were being exploited by violent elements — and took aim at the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) party and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
"There is a political hijacking of the blockades by elected officials from France Unbowed," he said.
Earlier on Monday, Mélenchon had accused the government of implementing a "crackdown" with "obvious racist undertones."
"Hands off our youth!" he wrote on social media, while encouraging LFI activists and officials to support the protests wherever they could.

Prime Minister Lecornu called the accusation of racism "an insult" and accused Mélenchon of "racializing a debate about student security and adding to division where a responsible politician should be looking to restore calm."
In the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, the LFI-run local council called the students' demands "legitimate" and published a statement reading:

"Let [the authorities] come and talk to [the students] and see for themselves whether the youth are being instrumentalized, or whether they are simply capable of thinking, organizing themselves and defending their own study conditions and their future."
France: The camps under Paris bridges
France: strikes — and an election — to come

The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, the French union that defends the interests of high school students, said it would urge a nationwide blockade of schools on Tuesday — coinciding with planned strike action by public sector workers.
French primary school teachers' unions said they expected some 40% of teachers to be off work on Tuesday.

With a key presidential election only seven months away and incumbent President Emmanuel Macron constitutionally barred from standing for a third term, French politicians from across the ideological spectrum are seeking issues that resonate with voters.
Mélenchon, a 75-year-old veteran anti-capitalist who finished third in the 2022 presidential election, is popular among younger, left-leaning voters.

His LFI party was one of the left-wing outfits which joined the Nouveau Front Populaire (New Popular Front or NFP) coalition in 2024 to oppose the far-right Rassemblement National (National Rally or RN) in legislative elections.
The coalition beat the RN but the elections produced a divided parliament which has been dogged by political deadlock and votes of no-confidence.

Prime Minister Lecornu is still trying to build enough support to pass a 2027 state budget, but his government is besieged by opponents who are unwilling to accept spending cuts while energy costs continue to rise.
Leo makes first official papal visit to France in 18 years

articles.title: OpenAI scraps release of new AI model over safety concerns
articles.summary: OpenAI has scrapped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, a next-generation artificial intelligence model planned for an October debut, after internal testing found the system did not meet the company's…

image.caption: OpenAI confirmed Monday it is scrapping its planned release of GPT-6.1 Astra, citing safety concerns. (Carlos Barria/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

OpenAI has scrapped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, a next-generation artificial intelligence model planned for an October debut, after internal testing found the system did not meet the company's ‌safety and alignment standards, the ChatGPT maker confirmed on Monday.
Company says internal testing determined GPT-6.1 Astra didn't meet safety standards
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and rival Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei earlier this month joined industry leaders in calling for a slower pace ​of AI development and stronger safety measures.

OpenAI has ​warned that Astra, its flagship GPT-6 model, can at times evade human oversight, while the company and rivals such as ​Anthropic have faced scrutiny over experimental AI systems that breached ⁠safeguards, including an ⁠OpenAI model that accessed Australia's health system ‌database.

The Wall Street Journal reported earlier in the day that OpenAI had abandoned plans to launch the model, which was expected to be integrated into ChatGPT and Codex and was designed to handle ⁠more complex tasks without human assistance.
OpenAI’s AI went rogue at least 4 times. This researcher caught 3 of them | Hanomansing Tonight

The Journal reported that GPT-6.1 Astra also showed higher levels of deception than its predecessor in internal testing, including instances in ‌which it did not always accurately disclose what actions it had taken.

items: Bill Gates joins call for AI safeguards, wants to discuss concerns with Trump
OpenAI pauses training of latest models after AI agents probed U.S. government sites in unexpected ways

blocks.text: "While [GPT-6.1 Astra] improved on axes such as model laziness, it didn't quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and ​authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done," ⁠said Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI.

"Of course we want ⁠to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's ⁠in ⁠the company, or when ​we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have ​an extremely high bar ⁠in terms of safety and alignment," Jain said.
The decision comes just ahead of OpenAI's developer conference in San Francisco, where the company has previously unveiled products aimed at software developers.

articles.title: Lost songs from iconic Australian rockstar found in garage
articles.summary: Divinyls frontwoman Chrissy Amphlett recorded the songs with Split Enz's Tim Finn in 1998.

blocks.text: More than a decade after her death, the voice of Australian rock icon Chrissy Amphlett will be heard like never before after three lost songs were discovered in a garage.

The trailblazing frontwoman of rock band Divinyls, Amphlett's trademark husky voice and charismatic stage presence brought the world the 1990 number one track I Touch Myself as well as earlier hits Pleasure and Pain (1985) and Boys in Town (1981).

Years before her 2013 death, Amphlett recorded three songs with Tim Finn, former lead singer of New Zealand's Split Enz, in 1998. The tracks were thought to be lost until Finn found them in his garage in 2023.
On Friday, the songs will be released in an EP titled Some Times.
In an interview with Australian Story, a documentary programme by national broadcaster ABC, Finn recalled the 1998 recording session with Amphlett in Sydney.
"It was a good time for us to meet because she was looking for something new, something different in her life musically," Finn said.

Around that time, Amphlett had split with fellow band member, guitarist Mark McEntee after a tumultuous relationship and was growing close to drummer Charley Drayton, according to the documentary. The pair would later marry.
Over several days, he and Amphlett wrote a trio of songs and headed into the studio to record them, with Drayton on the drums.
"She was so focused," Finn said. "She just wanted to get it right... I was in the presence of great talent, great charisma."
In a social media post on Monday about the 1998 session, Finn said he had reached out to Amphlett having been a great admirer of her work.
"We hadn't met previously but instantly felt a bond, a camaraderie of shared history as ex-lead singers of two brilliant bands," Finn wrote on Monday.
When the session wrapped up, Finn took the recordings home and planned to work on it, but "they were never fully realised".
In 2023, Drayton contacted Finn, about the 1998 recordings.

"I thought they were lost to the universe but remarkably found the two-inch tape in my garage," Finn wrote in the post, describing the songs as "incredibly important to me, Charley and those close to Chrissy".
"It was still in perfect condition and we are now able to share these songs with you."

articles.title: OpenAI scraps rollout of new model over safety concerns
articles.summary: The AI giant's safety chief said the model 'didn't quite meet the bar' of the firm's security standards.

blocks.text: OpenAI will not release its next-generation model - GPT-6.1 Astra - due to safety concerns, the ChatGPT-maker confirmed on Tuesday.
The AI system - which performs tasks like browsing the web and using apps by itself - "didn't quite meet the bar" of the company's standards, Saachi Jain, head of safety systems at OpenAI, said.

In recent weeks, top AI leaders including OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic boss Dario Amodei have urged the industry to slow the pace of development due to concerns about risks associated with the technology.
The debate around those risks has intensified in recent weeks after models developed by top AI firms were involved in a number of incidents.
OpenAI's decision, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, is a rare instance of a major AI developer pulling a new release over safety concerns.
The latest model fell short in terms of "staying within scope and authorisation, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done," Jain said.

"We want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users. But when we ship it to users, we have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment," she added.

The flagship GPT-6 Astra agentic model was released in September and specialises in complex reasoning and executing tasks autonomously. OpenAI said it was the result of "years of research and big bets".
The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after several high-profile incidents involving its technology.

Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that a rogue OpenAI agent had hacked into a government website in June and accessed private data in what experts said was the first known case of its kind in the world.

In July, OpenAI said its AI systems had accessed the internet and hacked into open-source developer hub Hugging Face, prompting researchers and officials to call for tighter controls over the technology.
On Monday, AI chip giant Nvidia released a set of software safety tools for autonomous AI platforms - called agents - that it said could have prevented the Hugging Face hack.
One of the new tools uses hardware features in Nvidia's chips to contain agents.
Nvidia boss Jensen Huang has largely dismissed calls for tighter AI regulations, arguing that rogue agents are an engineering problem that can be solved.
Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.9bn (£9.74bn) earlier this month.

articles.title: Israel's Netanyahu holds secret meeting with UAE president
articles.summary: After confirming a rare meeting, Netanyahu's office has denied suggestions that the Israeli prime minister requested that Abu Dhabi deny reports that it had warned Israel about an impending Hamas…

image.caption: It is the first time that the UAE has officially acknowledged a meeting between the two leadersImage: picture alliance

blocks.text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secretly met with the president of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, in Abu Dhabi on Sunday, both governments confirmed late on Monday.
"The two sides discussed bilateral relations between the UAE and Israel and ways to strengthen and develop them," read an Emirati statement.
Netanyahu's office said the visit "focused on strengthening relations between the two countries and on regional challenges."

The secret trip came weeks after a bombshell Israeli media report that the UAE president had warned Netanyahu about an imminent threat from the Palestinian militant group Hamas ahead of the deadly attack on Israel on October 7, 2023 — a warning which the Israeli premier allegedly failed to pass on to security services.
Indeed, Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported on Monday that the purpose of Netanyahu's visit had been to request that Sheikh Mohamed deny having given such a warning.
Netanyahu's office denied that the prime minister had made any such request, just as it had also denied the original report.
Netanyahu files complaint against Israeli broadcaster

Earlier on Monday, before the confirmation of Netanyahu's trip, Israel's domestic security service Shin Bet filed a complaint against Channel 12, accusing it of violating censorship rules by reporting the visit before the prime minister had returned to Israel.

"This evening, Shin Bet filed a complaint with the Chief Military Censor, demanding that Channel 12 be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law following a severe censorship violation," read a statement from Netanyahu's office.

It noted that the report had been made public while the premier's plane was still outside Israeli airspace and therefore "endangered the lives of the prime minister and his wife, as well as the delegation, which included the head of the Mossad" spy agency and other top security officials.
How the Iran war has deepened Saudi-UAE rivalry
Israel and the UAE: diplomatic relations

Sheikh Mohamed's hosting of Netanyahu was a significant development at a time when the Israeli leader is seen by many across the Middle East as the chief propagator of the war in Gaza, which has seen over 70,000 Palestinians killed — many of them civilians.
It is also the first time that the UAE has officially acknowledged a meeting between the two leaders after denying reports of a previous Netanyahu trip in May.
The UAE is one of only a handful of Arab nations which maintain official diplomatic ties with Israel after signing the Abraham Accords during US President Donald Trump's first term in 2020.
The UAE condemned the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023 as a "serious and grave escalation" and said it was "appalled" by reports of Israeli citizens being taken hostage.
But relations have also been strained by Israel's subsequent war in Gaza, with the UAE denouncing "ongoing Israeli violations" in the Palestinian enclave.

Nevertheless, Israel reportedly deployed Iron Dome air defense systems, together with personnel to operate them, to the UAE during the war against Iran, as the Gulf state faced retaliatory attacks from Tehran.

articles.title: Sign before praying: A new conversion law is affecting churchgoers in Indian state
articles.summary: A new anti-conversion law in Maharashtra is raising questions about faith, choice and freedom.

blocks.text: Sign before praying: A new conversion law is affecting churchgoers in Indian state
Image source, AFP via Getty Images
A new anti-conversion law in Maharashtra has sparked fears among Christians
ByJanhavee MooleBBC Marathi, Mumbai and Zoya MateenBBC News, Delhi
Some churches in and around India's financial capital Mumbai have begun asking worshippers to give a declaration in writing - "I came here to pray of my own free will."

Visitors write down their names, sometimes add an ID card number, and sign to say that nobody forced or enticed them to attend church. The forms, a copy of which the BBC has seen, have no official standing. Churches keep them in case a prayer meeting is challenged and its organisers are accused of trying to convert those inside.
The practice began at some churches in late August, just before a new law against religious conversion took effect in Maharashtra state, of which Mumbai is the capital.

The law prohibits religious conversions brought about by force, fraud, coercion or inducement. It also requires people who want to convert voluntarily to notify authorities in advance. An unlawful conversion can lead to a prison sentence of up to seven years, rising to 10 for a repeat offence.
Maharashtra's government says the law protects people, particularly those who are socially or economically vulnerable, from being forced or deceived into changing their religion.

But critics say its broad definitions, severe penalties and scrutiny of even voluntary conversions risk drawing the state and the police into one of the most private decisions a person can make. The state government did not respond to the BBC's repeated requests for comment.

While the law applies to all religions, the anxiety is being felt most deeply at places where minorities, especially Christians, worship. At the heart of the debate is a long-running tension over allegations, usually made by right-wing groups, about people being coerced or induced to change their religion for benefits.
Devdan Tribhuvan has seen some of that anxiety up close.

A fourth-generation Christian in Vasai, a suburb of Mumbai, he is part of an organisation that provides legal aid to Christians in and around the city. In recent months, he says, people have increasingly approached him not about court cases, but with accounts of disrupted prayer meetings and questions about what they are still free to do.
Some have described strangers walking into churches and questioning those inside: "What is your name? Why are you here? Has anyone offered you something?"

blocks.caption: Image caption, People from all religions visit the famous Mount Mary Church in Mumbai

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
People from all religions visit the famous Mount Mary Church in Mumbai
The questions can become more pointed, Tribhuvan said, when a worshipper has a name that does not sound Christian: "Has anyone forced you to come? Has anyone offered you an inducement?"
Many who contact him are not looking to take legal action. They want to know whether simply gathering to pray could leave them vulnerable to an accusation of conversion.

In July, an investigation by The Indian Express, external documented five disruptions of Christian prayer meetings around Mumbai between April and July. Nine police cases followed - seven against worshippers or prayer organisers, and two against members of the Hindu nationalist group Bajrang Dal. Police did not respond to detailed questions about the cases or the action taken.
"Is gathering for prayer itself conversion?" Tribhuvan asks.

In Mumbai, Tribhuvan's question carries particular weight. The city grew by drawing people from across India and beyond, bringing their gods and rituals with them. A church bell can sound within earshot of a mosque's call to prayer; a shrine belonging to one faith can draw followers of another.

People of many faiths make their way to the Muslim shrine Haji Ali. Hindus light candles at Mount Mary, a Catholic basilica overlooking the city. Crowds fill the streets around Lalbaug during the Hindu festival of Ganesh Chaturthi and stream to Siddhivinayak temple throughout the year.

Maharashtra is the latest of more than a dozen states to restrict religious conversion. The laws differ, but their reach has expanded in recent years, particularly in states governed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party. Several are being challenged before the Supreme Court.

Behind that expansion lie claims long made by Hindu nationalist groups, that Christians use money, schooling or medical care to draw poor and tribal communities away from Hinduism, and that Muslim men court Hindu women to convert them - an alleged conspiracy they call "love jihad."

blocks.caption: Image caption, A bunch of anti-conversion laws in Indian states have made interfaith marriages more challenging

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
A bunch of anti-conversion laws in Indian states have made interfaith marriages more challenging

Critics say such accusations have fuelled harassment of Christian prayer meetings and interfaith couples, and that the laws give those making them a way to draw the police into questions of prayer, marriage and belief.
Maharashtra's government says the new law leaves people free to convert by choice, while addressing what it says is a rise in forced conversions that existing laws have failed to curb.
Critics question where it draws the line between force and choice.

"We do not support forceful conversions, if any," said Samsuddin Tamboli, president of the Muslim Satyashodhak Mandal (Muslim Truth-seeking Society), a reformist organisation. His concern is what the law counts as inducement.

Its definition of "allurement" includes employment, free education at a religious institution, a promise of marriage, a "better lifestyle" and "divine healing". Even glorifying one religion over another can fall within it.
"The definition has been kept so vague that almost any benefit accruing to a person can be considered or argued to be an allurement," said Abhay Thipsay, a retired Bombay High Court judge.
"If a person receives some benefit and consciously chooses to convert for that reason, why should it be considered wrong?"

The law also allows parents, siblings and other relatives to complain to police about an allegedly unlawful conversion, leaving the person accused of causing or assisting it to prove that it was lawful.
Critics say for interfaith couples, that provision adds another potential obstacle to marriages that can already face family opposition.

Indian law allows people of different faiths to marry without converting, but requires a month's notice. Lara Jesani, a lawyer who has helped interfaith couples obtain court protection, said details of planned weddings have sometimes reached relatives and Hindu nationalist groups opposed to them within that notice period.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Critics fear the new law may give families or right-wing organisations a new way to target interfaith couples

blocks.text: Critics fear the new law may give families or right-wing organisations a new way to target interfaith couples
In cases she has handled, she said, families have taken women away, even from the marriage registrar's office.
Now, she fears the new law may give the families or right-wing organisations a new way to target such couples.
"Even when neither intend to convert, [the couples] fear a relative could accuse one partner of trying to convert the other."

The Maharashtra government did not respond to detailed questions from the BBC about these concerns. But when the law was passed, state minister Pankaj Bhoyar said it did not infringe upon the right to change religion. The notification requirement, he said, was intended to establish whether a conversion was voluntary, while allowing the state to act against those brought about by fraud, coercion or inducement.
But Tribhuvan is still worried, an anxiety, he says, which reaches even the small prayer gatherings held closer to home when a church is too far away.
Fifty people might attend, he said, sometimes 100 - and someone who is not Christian might join too.
"If someone else wishes to come and pray, we cannot stop them," he said. "That is what we call the right to choose."
To Thipsay, the retired judge, the precaution points to a larger question.
"If an adult has the power to make major decisions - such as whom to marry - and has been given the right to vote," he said, "why should they not have the power to make this decision too?"

articles.title: Journalist to be crowned king in Uganda after bitter succession dispute
articles.summary: Kijanangoma is being crowned amid a dispute over a young heir whom the royal clan does not recognise.

blocks.text: Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo II, who is set to be crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom later, has long been a familiar face in the country.
For many Ugandans, he was known not as the heir to the throne, but as a storyteller, as a long-serving anchor and editor at the state broadcaster.
But Kijanangoma, 56, has now become the subject of media attention himself - his rise to the Tooro throne sparking controversy and widespread reactions beyond the country.

Tooro is one of Uganda's four main officially recognised historical kingdoms. For the last 31 years, it has been headed by King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who was once known as a "boy king", after ascending to the throne as an infant.
Oyo became king in 1995 at the age of just three, following the death of his father. Then the world's youngest monarch, he ruled until he died last month from cancer, aged just 34.

The coronation is a day for celebration, involving traditional practices starting from midnight. The new king then walks about 4km (2.5 miles) to the official Karuziika royal palace where he is crowned.

A mock fight follows, to signify that kingship does not come easy, and he is then blessed by members of the royal Babiito clan, the Tooro kingdom's Information Minister Charles Mwanguhya told the BBC Focus on Africa podcast.

He performs other ceremonies that signifies his assumption of the throne, before he sits on the throne and an actual crown placed on his head to signify his new authority, his new position as the new Tooro king.
But the selection of Kijanangoma as king was far from straightforward.

According to tradition, a recognised son of the late king should succeed him. Close members of the royal family said Oyo had left a young son and a will with instructions that the child should be next on the throne.
But the son has never been revealed to the public and nor was he recognised by the committee of 21 Babiito clan members who choose the king and eventually selected Kijanangoma.
The late King Oyo was never publicly married, and little is known about his wife or their son.
Nonetheless his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, argued that the late king's will ought to have been respected.
However, the royal succession committee ignored her wishes, insisting their selection process was conducted in accordance with Tooro customs and traditions.
The new king has thus found himself at the centre of a succession dispute, with Kemigisa and her close relatives unhappy with the outcome.
Kemigisa referred to Kijanangoma's selection as the "announcement of a second king" being "made after the will of King Oyo was read to members of the royal family".
"As a mother, that was extraordinarily painful," she said, describing celebrations for the next king taking place "only metres from where my son's body lay".
The queen later said Oyo's son, who was in the US state of Texas, had been due to return home but that could not happen amid a "tense and polarised succession dispute".
"No child should be placed in circumstances where returning to his father's homeland could mean being drawn into hostility and conflict," Kemigisa asserted in a post on X.

But according to the Tooro kingdom's information minister, the son being talked about "hasn't been presented anywhere, which means there is a growing acceptance that sad as it may be, King Oyo didn't leave a son behind".
While King Oyo inherited the crown from his father, Mwanguhya told the BBC "the crown has moved to a different line within the ruling clan".
A king must come from the Babiito clan, specifically the lineage of King George David Matthew Kamurasi Rukidi III, according to royal palace sources.
Kijanangoma and the late King Oyo are cousins. Both are grandsons of Rukidi III, the 11th king, or Omukama, who ruled the Tooro kingdom from 1928 to 1965.
Kijanangoma was among several people who were considered for the role, including Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, who plays football for one of the UK's best-known amateur clubs.
According to the succession committee, the South East Dons captain and goalkeeper declined the offer of the throne, citing other responsibilities.
After he was formally announced, Kijanangoma promised that the palace would be open to the people, while vowing to focus on unity and development.
"I ask you for one thing - they have given me this title as king but I cannot work alone, I have to work with you," he said.
Uganda's traditional kings have no formal political authority, but they retain cultural influence and command significant loyalty in the communities they lead.
The country is home to four main kingdoms, the largest and most prominent being Buganda in the central region, which encompasses the capital Kampala.
The kingdoms were abolished in 1967, but the government under President Yoweri Museveni restored them in the early 1990s.
The government said this was to promote cultural pride and national unity, but the move has also been interpreted as a way of appeasing communities and fostering political loyalty.

Amid the succession dispute, the government backed the Babiito clan's choice of Kijanangoma. Attorney General Sam Mayanja said the Tooro kingdom was cleared to go ahead with the coronation, as there had not been a formal complaint against him.
The date of the coronation was announced by the government and Museveni is scheduled to attend.
The president's son and the head of the military, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has also publicly supported Kijanangoma. "Long may he reign," he posted on X.
Kijanangoma's very name points to his royal heritage.
His father, the first Kijanangoma, was born in the year King Rukidi III became king. The king gave him the name, which means the "one who comes with the royal drum".
The drum of royalty, foretold two generations earlier, is now returning to its bearer.
Kijanangoma was born in 1970 and raised at their family home at Kidukuru village in Fort Portal, about 300 km (186 miles) from Kampala.
He left the village to pursue further studies and graduated with a mass communication degree from Uganda's prestigious Makerere University in 1999.
He worked as a broadcaster in a career spanning more than two decades, including in neighbouring Rwanda and at home, with the Uganda Broadcasting Corporation.

The years spent engaging with the public, the interactions with leaders and the exposure to national affairs in his work as a journalist may yet serve him well as he returns to the community he came from, this time as their leader.
After he was named king, Kijanangoma said he would use the connections he had built up over 21 years working as a journalist "to get good things for our people".
His mother, Assimwe Yusta Kijanangoma, is confident that he is well prepared for his new role. She says his upbringing was deeply rooted in tradition.
"I really raised him with the teachings of the old kingdom of a cane and instructions and scolding. I laugh with him, and other times I scold him," she told the BBC.
She added: "Eddy is well-mannered, he does not fight, or shout, even when wronged, he says a few words and does not go so much into it."
She feels good for her son, although she admits to having mixed emotions, especially as her son is taking over after the death of a "great man".

articles.title: Election lawyer seeks TRO vs law moving barangay, SK polls to 2028
articles.summary: He asks the Supreme Court to strike down the law moving the polls to 2028.

blocks.text: September 29, 2026 | 7:30am
MANILA, Philippines — Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal asked the Supreme Court to strike down the law postponing the November 2026 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections to November 2028.

Macalintal filed a petition for certiorari and prohibition on Monday, September 28 challenging the constitutionality of Republic Act 12326, naming the Office of the President, Senate, House of Representatives and Commission on Elections as respondents.
He also sought an immediate status quo ante order, temporary restraining order and writ of preliminary injunction to halt the law's implementation.
"I thought 'forever' was only in love. Turns out 'forever' also exists in barangay election postponements," Macalintal told reporters in Filipino at the Supreme Court grounds.
"That is why we will fight this, because this postponement is far too long. And our right to vote was taken away from us by our lawmakers," he added.
'Whimsical' 3-year delay
Macalintal argued that the law infringes on the electorate's right of suffrage under the guise of "fixing" the term of barangay officials at five years.
The last BSKE was held on Oct. 30, 2023, while the next elections were originally scheduled for December 2025.
Congress later moved the polls to November 2026 through Republic Act 12232, which also adjusted the term of office to four years.
Republic Act 12326, meanwhile, postpones the elections by another two years to November 2028, resulting in a cumulative three-year delay from the original December 2025 schedule.
Macalintal argued that the repeated deferrals deprives voters of their right to vote for an unreasonably long period.

The delay, he said, is a "very clear grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of Congress." He also called the postponement "very apparent arbitrary and whimsical," citing Macalintal v. Senate and Macalintal v. COMELEC.
'Lightning speed'
Macalintal also questioned how quickly the law was enacted.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Republic Act 12326 on September 24, with the law taking effect immediately upon its publication the following day.

"It was practically enacted at lightning speed, mabilis pa sa kidlat, or in apparent haste, and with the clear and direct effect of shutting the courthouse doors to Petitioner and similarly situated citizens, leaving them with a dangerously narrow window to study, research, and draft a well-founded petition, considering that the November 2, 2026 BSKE is barely one month and a few days away," Macalintal said.
He also challenged the administration's justifications for postponement, including the use of incumbent officials to help fight crime, manage floods and coordinate garbage disposal.

Macalintal argued that these are routine administrative functions that do not meet what he described as the strict constitutional standards for postponing elections established in Macalintal v. Comelec.
He also questioned justifications raised during congressional deliberations involving funding risks from the global oil crisis and conflicts in the Middle East.
Macalintal pointed out that those external crises did not prevent the government from holding the Sept. 14, 2026 elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.
He also cited the Comelec's declaration that it was fully prepared for the November 2026 BSKE, arguing that postponement would waste billions of pesos already spent on preparations.
Holdover provision challenged
Beyond the postponement itself, Macalintal also challenged the law's transitory provision, which treats the holdover period of incumbent officials as a completed term.

He argued that the provision conflates "term of office" with "tenure of office" and effectively amounts to the legislative appointment of holdover officials, contrary to the constitutional requirement that barangay officials be elected.
The law, he said, effectively creates a "two-year term extension" without clearly identifying the provision that grants it.

articles.title: Melbourne human rights activist disappears in Cambodia as wife urges Albanese government help
articles.summary:
Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Australian Vietnamese anti-human trafficking campaigner, not heard from since 18 September

The wife of an Australian activist missing in Cambodia has implored the…

blocks.text: The wife of an Australian activist missing in Cambodia has implored the federal government to find him and bring him home.

Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Australian Vietnamese democracy campaigner, was due to return to Bangkok, Thailand, to reunite with his wife Chloe Dang after a short trip to Phnom Penh, Cambodia, to meet with human rights defenders.
But he never boarded his flight and has not communicated with his wife since 18 September, leaving her worried for his safety.
“My family and I are really worried about his safety, and we just only want to know where he is and what happened to him,” Dang said from Bangkok airport before boarding a flight to Melbourne.
“My husband deserves protection, and I really hope the Australian government will continue to put pressure on Cambodia to do an investigation to find out where he is right now.”

Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, was travelling with another human rights activist Nguyen Duc Thuan, who is also Vietnamese and holds a Norwegian passport.
The pair travelled to Cambodia to meet with dissident Vietnamese activists for training.

blocks.caption: Tran Hiep has not communicated with his wife since 18 September

blocks.text: Vietnam in recent years has ramped up its crackdown on dissidents, with more than 55 activists arrested under broad criminal laws in 2025.
Civil society groups and United Nations human rights experts have repeatedly warned of growing co-operation between Vietnamese authorities and neighbouring governments targeting advocates.

Viet Tan, a pro-democracy diaspora political party, has described the pair’s disappearance as concerning given previous cases involving Vietnamese dissidents vanishing in neighbouring countries and subsequently appearing in custody in Vietnam.
“Their disappearance is not an ordinary ‘missing person’ incident. Both men are long-time human rights advocates and Viet Tan members,” the organisation said.
Dang, 36, said fretting over her husband’s whereabouts had taken a psychological toll.
“It’s been 11 days and I’m really in the dark,” she said, choking back tears.
“I don’t know where he is and how he’s doing – it’s driving me crazy.
“Everything is really uncertain.”
The Australian government confirmed consular officials were in contact with Dang but declined to comment further.
“The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian reported missing in Cambodia,” a department spokesperson said on Monday.
The families of the missing men have filed an appeal with the UN working group on enforced or involuntary disappearances.

articles.title: Tennessee governor rejects clemency bid for Christa Pike as execution looms
articles.summary: If the execution proceeds, Pike would be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

blocks.text: "After deliberate consideration of Christa Gail Pike's request for clemency, and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding the sentence of the State of Tennessee and do not plan to intervene," Governor Lee said in a statement.
Pike's legal team had filed the clemency petition earlier this month, requesting that her death sentence be commuted to life in prison.

Moving ahead with Pike's execution puts Tennessee "on singular footing", her attorneys said, as she would be the first person the state "executes in the modern death penalty era who was a teenager at the time of the offence".
Attorneys Stephen Ferrell, Kelly Gleason and Randy Spivey said the governor's decision "leaves unanswered vital questions about Tennessee's execution protocol".

"With this decision, the State of Tennessee is ignoring what both science and our legal system have decided: an 18-year-old brain is not an adult brain, and 18 is too young to face execution," they said in a statement on Monday.
The murder of Colleen Slemmer created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the 19-year-old was found with a pentagram - a symbol of Satanic ritual - carved into her chest.

Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.
A year later, she was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death, while then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp- who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
At the time of her incarceration, the 21-year-old was the youngest person on death row, according to the Tennessee Department of Corrections.
Pike is scheduled to be executed on 30 September after years of failed appeals.
Colleen's mother has insisted she wants Pike's execution to move forward so that her daughter "finally can be resting".

articles.title: What to know about Cornell's alleged frat house gang-rape case and the 'Cornell 7'
articles.summary: Investigators in New York are reopening an investigation into an alleged gang rape at Cornell University after a woman filed a lawsuit claiming the university didn't do enough to protect her.

image.caption: A student walks past a Cornell University sign in Ithaca, N.Y., Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. (Heather Ainsworth/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: WARNING: This article may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it. It also contains vulgar language.

Alumni are threatening to pull funding, celebrities are lashing out and people are boycotting institutions associated with an alleged gang rape at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., currently igniting the internet.

The case came into the spotlight after the victim, known only as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16, alleging the private Ivy League university protected the seven men, now dubbed "the Cornell 7." She claims they drugged and assaulted her over several hours at a frat house in October 2024.

The lawsuit, filed in New York Supreme Court and viewed by CBC News, alleges the assault happened on campus at the Chi Phi Fraternity house, and that one of the frat brothers sent a Snapchat message inviting other members to join them for "free pussy."
It further claims that the accused only faced temporary suspensions and "were afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays" to the university — a claim Cornell denies.

None of the fraternity members have been criminally charged. But the case has unleashed online fury, drawing comparisons to last year's Hockey Canada sexual assault trial in London, Ont., which saw all five players acquitted.
On Monday, the Tompkins County district attorney announced he was reopening the investigation.

"Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means available — by testimony to the Tompkins County grand jury," district attorney Matthew Van Houten told CBC News in a written statement.

Cornell, in its own statement Monday, said it supported the DA's decision for a criminal grand jury to hear the woman's claims, but disputed the lawsuit's allegations about how the university punished the accused.
"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," Kyle Kimball, vice-president for university relations, said in a statement posted online.
The statement also said the on-campus Chi Phi chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.
Here's what to know about the case and why it's caused so much fury online.
What's in the lawsuit?

According to the lawsuit, the assault began the night of Oct. 19, 2024. Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time, had been drinking with her sorority, and again at a nightclub and then "stumbled" alone at 11 p.m. to the Chi Phi fraternity house on campus to visit a friend — one of the accused.

"Plaintiff was visibly intoxicated as she had consumed about 10 standard drinks within the past three hours," the lawsuit says. It also says the nightclub served the woman "at least one" alcoholic beverage even though it had marked an X on her hand showing she was underage.
At the frat house, she was given a beer, and her friend allegedly proposed a threesome with another member, to which she was too intoxicated to consent, the suit states.

The accused allegedly took her upstairs and led her to a room with another of the accused. She was pressured to snort ketamine, the lawsuit alleges, adding that she had never used that substance before. They also "plied her" with cannabis and rum, it says, after which the two men "began engaging in sexual acts with plaintiff, all without her consent."

items: Hockey Canada sexual assault trial 'reinvigorated' talk on complex issues of consent, sports culture
Intense backlash in Edmonton greets Oilers signing of Alex Formenton

blocks.text: As they engaged in oral and vaginal sex, one of the accused also repeatedly slapped her buttocks, resulting in bruising, the lawsuit says. One of the men left to have a nap, and another entered the room. The two remaining men then began another alleged assault on the woman.

At 1:42 a.m., one of them sent a Snapchat message to the rest of the fraternity, claiming there was "free pussy." The suit includes an image of the alleged message, and some of the purported responses from the accused, including, "like you can walk in and whip it out."
Text messages and consent at the Hockey Canada sex assault trial

According to the suit, "multiple" other fraternity members then entered the room. One of them allegedly put ketamine on his erect penis and told the woman to snort it, which she did. The men then began snorting the substance off her naked body, the suit states. Two men took her to another room, where they allegedly assaulted her again.

The alleged incident ended at 5:45 a.m., and Jane Doe passed out. She returned to her sorority house "in a state of shock," the documents state, and soon realized the events were becoming "public knowledge" on campus.

She reported it a few weeks later to the Cornell University Police Department around Nov. 8, 2024. She alleges the seven accused were issued temporary suspensions and allowed "to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays."
The university released a statement and investigated, but ultimately closed it at a later date, according to the lawsuit.

Jane Doe suffered "severe emotional and psychological distress and personal physical injury" due to the alleged assault and the university's purported handling of it, the lawsuit says. She is suing the seven men, the Chi Phi fraternity, the university, Moonies Bar and Nightclub and others, seeking undisclosed damages.
The seven Chi Phi members named in the lawsuit are Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar.
"Ms. Doe has had her dreams destroyed as a result of what has happened to her," her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told CBC News in a written statement.
"The fact that her trauma has been made public has been very difficult. However, she has been gratified by the outpouring of support that she has received from the public."
Online backlash to 'the culture of rape'

As the lawsuit made headlines, the backlash was swift. Online, Cornell alumni called on each other to stop donating to the school. Some people publicly turned down their acceptances, and others launched campaigns targeting the university, the local police and the various workplaces of the so-called "Cornell 7."
The seven accused were outed by Cornell's student newspaper editorial board on Sept. 21 in an editorial titled, "Cornell won't, we will."

A former South Park writer launched a website to expose the accused. Actors Josh Gad and Florence Pugh posted online condemning the alleged assault and what the lawsuit described as the university's handling of it.
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez condemned what she called a "culture of rape" at elite institutions while speaking about the alleged incident, at a town hall in Ithaca over the weekend.
"This is a culture, this is norms, these are practices," said Ocasio-Cortez, according to the Cornell Daily Sun. “What we must do is understand that we cannot protect those spaces anymore.”
Cornell's response
The university said in a statement Monday that it conducted its own investigation at the time and issued sanctions, including expelling some students and suspending others.
In response to the claims, Cornell said "none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement."

The school said it conducted an internal disciplinary investigation in 2024. It said a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days, and both the woman and the accused testified and presented evidence.
In a statement last week responding to the lawsuit, Cornell said federal privacy law barred it from disclosing specific information on individual students.
Reopening the case

Van Houten, the district attorney, said Monday that in light of the attention the case has received, he wanted to clarify why the original investigation did not result in criminal charges. He said that Jane Doe went to campus police at the time, but did not, in her initial sworn statement, make any claims of being gang-raped or drugged.
"On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual," he said.
The prosecutor also said the woman's attorney did not contact him about her statement or about reconsidering the decision not to prosecute.
'She was traumatized'
Giuffra, Jane Doe's lawyer, defended his client while blaming the university police investigation.
"In the days following the assault, she was traumatized, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened. She was in self-preservation mode," Giuffra told CBC News.
He questioned why she wasn't contacted by the DA's office or any investigators trained in interviewing rape survivors.

items: Interactive: Campus sexual assault reports
Ryerson, Acadia University statements on CBC's campus sexual assaults report

blocks.text: "It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted when she ... never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her original complaint," Giuffra added.

Multiple media now report that the seven accused men have sought legal representation. CBC News has reached out to Jeremy Saland, one of the lawyers identified, and has not yet heard back. But Saland told BBC his client denies the allegations.

His client "responded to and made an immature comment on Snapchat," but "did nothing else," the outlet reported. Saland said his client "was involved in no sexual activity nor touched the plaintiff in any way and ingested no ketamine."

If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database. ​​

articles.title: French PM warns against escalation of school protests after 164 arrested
articles.summary: Students are protesting over issues such as overcrowded classes, but the prime minister has condemned reports of violence.

blocks.text: France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has warned that any escalation in the country's current wave of student protests would be "irresponsible", following the arrests of 164 people on Monday.
The demonstrations, which started in Paris and have seen teenagers blockading their schools for days, stem from issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages.
Lecornu cited reported incidents at protests in a post on X, saying: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers."
But a French union that defends the interests of high school students said the protests were a "legitimate response" to the conditions they face.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 12 members of the security forces, 12 students and three school staff were injured on Monday, while 180 schools were affected.
He did not provide further details on those who had been arrested.
The movement at French lycées, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Île-de-France region around Paris.
Incidents of vandalism were reported, along with fireworks being aimed at police, and the protests have now spread to other regions in France.

According to the AFP news agency, four high schools were reportedly blockaded in the southern regions of Alpes-Maritimes and Var. Protests have also been reported in Marseille, the northern Lille area and Sedan in the north-eastern Ardennes.
The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, which represents students, defended the protests in a post on social media.

"Lack of teachers and staff, dilapidated schools, overcrowded schedules and classes, stress caused by Parcoursup [the web platform used in France for students to apply to the first year of higher education]... These issues are by no means inevitable, but simply the result of 10 years of Macron's policies and the lack of resources in the national education system," it said.
It called on students to blockade schools on Tuesday in defence of "their rights and against budget austerity".
On the same day, unions representing teachers, hospital staff and civil servants also called for a day of walkouts to protest against issues including low wages and working conditions.

In response to the student movement, Lecornu said "the difficulties of high schools must be heard and addressed", but that "violence must be condemned unequivocally, and its perpetrators must answer for their actions".
The prime minister also accused the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of urging students to expand the movement.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, LFI's leader, blamed the Lecornu government for having "ordered the crackdown" on the protest, adding that the high school students taking part were "harmless".
But Nuñez said the demonstrations and blockades were "not very typical protest movements".

"It is much more like urban violence, with a number of individuals who were masked, equipped with fireworks in tubes, equipped with projectiles, who clearly wanted to confront the internal security forces," he said.
"It wasn't about making demands; it was really violence in its purest form."
Since the protests began, several incidents involving violence between students and police officers have been reported.
In one incident, a police officer reportedly fired a round from a grenade launcher used for crowd control, injuring a high school student, according to France's BFMTV.
Investigations have been launched into these incidents, the broadcaster added.

articles.title: Elephants may use medicinal plants to treat themselves and their babies
articles.summary: A new study taps into local knowledge to identify dozens of medicinal plants used elephants in the Mount Elgon region of Kenya. However, scientists caution that more research is needed.

image.caption: New research suggests African elephants in the Mount Elgon region of Kenya may use medicinal plants to treat themselves and their young. (Mount Elgon Foundation/Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine)

blocks.text: As It Happens
A new study taps into local knowledge to identify dozens of medicinal plants used elephants in the Mount Elgon region of Kenya. However, scientists caution that more research is needed.
Small study uses local knowledge to identify 35 medicinal plants used by elephants in Kenya
LISTEN | Interview with scientist Elodie Freymann:
As It Happens6:17Elephants may use medicinal plants to treat themselves and their babies

A sickly looking elephant chews the bark of a tree that's widely used in traditional medicine. A mother elephant mixes a plant with known medicinal properties with her milk and feeds it to her babies.
These are a few of the stories that researchers have gathered from local wildlife scouts and community members about African elephants in the Mount Elgon region of Kenya.
"I've stopped being surprised at this point," Elodie Freymann, who studies self-medication in the animal kingdom, told As It Happens guest host Helen Mann.

"Knowing how intelligent and complex elephants are and elephant societies are, it was just a matter of time, I think, before we began learning just about the extent of the diversity of the medicinal plants that elephants are using in the wild."
Freymann is the co-author of a new study, published Thursday in the journal Nature, that taps into local knowledge to document several dozen medicinal plants used by Mount Elgon elephants.
The researchers say the study adds to a growing body of evidence that elephants are complex and intelligent creatures, and demonstrates why it's important to protect the biodiversity they rely on.
However, scientists caution that more research is needed to say with certainty that the elephants are self-medicating.
Using local knowledge

The findings are based on interviews with eight members of the Sabaot community who have lived and worked with the elephants for decades, including wildlife scouts, community guides and village elders.

In some cases, they describe elephants who appear weak, lethargic or stomach sick seeking out specific plants that are used in local medicine. In other cases, they describe mother elephants feeding known medicinal plants to their young.

Of the 35 plants mentioned in the interviews, 34 are used locally in traditional medicine. Eight of the nine most commonly cited plants have been documented in scientific literature as having pharmacological properties.
"We went to the source. We went to people who have lived amongst these elephant populations for decades and decades," said Freymann, a post-doctoral fellow at Brown University in Rhode Island.
"I think Western science, for a very long time, hasn't championed those local voices, and it's time we start doing that."
More evidence needed

Chase LaDue, an elephant ecologist who was not involved in the research, said the study makes a great starting point for further research, but doesn't prove elephants are intentionally medicating themselves or their young.

"There were no health data showing any of these elephants were actually sick, and nobody measured whether eating these plants changed anything," LaDue, a curator at the Oklahoma City Zoo and the executive director of the Sri Lanka Elephant Project, said in an email.

"What young calves do all the time is put their trunks into their mothers' mouths and sample whatever she's chewing. It's one of the main ways they learn what to eat. It's possible something like that is being described here and understood through a medical lens. I'd want to see it before calling it medicine."
Local knowledge, he says, often points researchers in the right direction. But anecdotal evidence has its limits.

"If you grew up knowing a plant treats stomach trouble in people, and you see an elephant eat it, it's natural to connect the two. But elephants eat an enormous variety of plants. In a region this botanically rich, it would be surprising if many of them didn't have some traditional medicinal use," he said. "Overlap by itself doesn't tell us much."
Freymann says it's unlikely the elephants are eating medicinal plants simply out of personal preference because they tend to be full of compounds that taste bitter and awful.

"In small doses, they're medicines, but in high doses, they're poisons," she said. "They're the compounds that the plants generate as a defence against predators, like caterpillars, that are trying to eat them. "

But she agrees this study is just a starting point. Her team has outfitted the interviewees with cameras to document the elephants consuming the plants. She says studying that footage will be the next step in the research.
"We have an incredible, incredible launch pad for conducting further research on this," she said.

items: When an earthquake hit, these elephants formed a protective circle around their youngest
Elephants may have names for each other that humans don't know, study finds

blocks.text: If the researchers are able to prove the elephants are, indeed, self-medicating, they'll join a growing list of animals who exhibit similar behaviour, including chimpanzees and other great apes, and some insects and birds.
All the more reason to champion biodiversity, says Freymann.
"Habitat loss doesn't just mean the loss of foods for animals. It doesn't mean the loss of territory for animals. It also means the loss for medicine," she said.

"In this changing world with unstable climatic conditions and changing ecologies, it's more important than ever that animals have the access to the medicines that they need to flourish in their environment."
Interview with Elodie Freymann produced by Calan Pittis

articles.title: New York Times executive fatally shot allegedly by elderly in-laws
articles.summary: Jonathan McKinsey's in-laws, who are both 77 years old, face multiple charges including first-degree murder.

blocks.text: A New York Times executive was fatally shot in California, allegedly by his wife's elderly parents who have been arrested on suspicion of murder.

Jonathan McKinsey, 40, the newspaper's director of engineering for games player experience, was found with multiple gunshot wounds in a car park in Dublin - 35 miles (56km) west of San Francisco - on Saturday afternoon, police said.
Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, his parents-in-law who are both 77 years old, are facing multiple charges, including first-degree murder.
It was unclear whether the couple have a lawyer, and they are due to appear in court to formally face the charges on Wednesday.
McKinsey's death was confirmed by The New York Times.
His body was found at 15:00 (23:00 GMT) on Thursday afternoon outside the Dublin Sports Grounds.
Witnesses told KGO-TV in San Francisco that they heard a flurry of gunshots, before seeing the victim on the ground.
"I saw the guy drop to the floor: head bloody and chest bloody," witness Assad Razawi told the news outlet.
His daughter added that her father saw the couple "walking together and then casually walk away from the shooting".
The couple were arrested several minutes later by an officer passing by the scene. They had remained in the area after the attack, a witness said.
McKinsey was pronounced dead at the scene, according to police.
Police have not disclosed any motive for his killing.
The elderly couple are being held at the Santa Rita jail.
They also face charges of felony conspiracy, wilful discharge of a firearm with gross negligence, and child endangerment.
